item.title: Three killed, thousands evacuated as Cyclone Arnab hits eastern India - AsiaOne.com
item.summary: A satellite image shows Cyclone Arnab making landfall over the south-eastern coast of the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, Oct 27, in this still ...
item.page_text:
BHUBANESWAR/HYDERABAD, India — At least three people were killed, dozens of houses damaged and crops destroyed as a powerful cyclone struck India's eastern coast from the Bay of Bengal on Wednesday (Oct 28), bringing heavy rain and strong winds, authorities said.
Cyclone Arnab, classified by the India Meteorological Department as a very severe cyclonic storm — the third-highest category on its scale — made landfall in Andhra Pradesh state early on Wednesday, with its centre then moving fully inland, the agency said.
"Andhra Pradesh has been most affected ... three people have lost their lives," Narendra Singh Bundela, a top official at the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), told reporters.
Heavy rain and high winds destroyed at least 180 houses, brought down 220 trees and disrupted power supply in several areas, Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu said in a letter to federal Home Minister Amit Shah, updating him on the situation.
Two of the deaths were caused by a tree falling and electrocution, officials in Naidu's office told Reuters.
Neighbouring Odisha state was not as badly affected, Bundela said, adding that wind-speeds were expected to reduce as the cyclone moved inland.
More than 180,000 people had been evacuated in the states of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha ahead of the cyclone's arrival.
Some schools were closed and some train and flight services cancelled along the eastern coast.
Several NDRF and state teams were working in the affected areas, Bundela said, adding that some neighbouring states were also likely to be affected by heavy rain.
Television images showed trees fallen on highways as workers in rain gear worked to clear the road of branches and leaves.
"No one knew whose house the water would rush into next, or whose home would be submerged," said Nagi, a resident of Andhra's Kakinada district.
"Trees have fallen, houses have been damaged, and all our belongings, including our books, have been destroyed," said Nagi, who did not give a last name.
Fishermen along the coast had been advised against going out to sea, and the weather department said it anticipated losses to crops, as well as damage to thatched houses and communication lines.
Winds of 125 kph to 135 kph (77.7 mph to 83.9 mph) and gusts of up to 150 kph are forecast, with a storm surge of 1 metre to 1.5 metres (3.28 feet to 4.92 feet) above normal tide likely to inundate low-lying areas of Andhra Pradesh, it said.
Operations at three Andhra Pradesh airports were suspended, India's civil aviation ministry said.
In neighbouring Nepal, authorities suspended the issuing of trekking permits to high mountain areas for three days because of the risk of rain and blizzards due to the cyclone, Immigration Department information officer Gita Ghimire told Reuters.
This is peak trekking season in Nepal with around 750 hikers getting permits per day.
On Tuesday, Nepal warned tourists against venturing into high-altitude areas due to fears that Arnab could trigger torrential downpours, snowstorms and avalanches in the Himalayan region from Thursday night through Saturday.
Arnab formed over the Bay of Bengal, a major region for tropical cyclones that has spawned deadly storms on India's east coast.
A super cyclone that killed nearly 10,000 people when it hit Odisha in October 1999 remains one of the country's deadliest natural disasters.
India, however, has over the years developed early-warning systems and preventive measures to minimise loss of life.

item.title: Damaged Tanker Leaks Oil Across UAE Waters As Spill - Marine Link
item.summary: The images provided by the EU's Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellites showed a large oil spill coming from the tanker. Authorities across various ...
item.page_text:
An oil spill from a damaged tanker off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has widened, satellite images showed, triggering more beach closures and raising environmental concerns.
Images from the European Union's Copernicus satellite observation network dated October 24 show the oil spill has widened over the last few days and is reaching close to the shores of the northern Umm Al Quwain emirate, with dark layers of oil spreading at sea and along its coastline.
Since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have driven up security risks for maritime traffic and heightened fears over the conflict's environmental fallout.
October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy think tank.
The UAE said on Friday that efforts were under way to contain oil leaking from a tanker offshore, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment.
Authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill. But experts told Reuters that the spill was coming from a tanker called the Gem No.2, which shipping sources said was a vessel that had been struck by an unidentified projectile last month, causing a fire that was later extinguished.
The images provided by the EU's Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellites showed a large oil spill coming from the tanker.
Authorities across various northern emirates responded to the spill by restricting access to coastal areas.
The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Friday that all beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain were temporarily closed, while authorities in neighbouring Sharjah shut access to Al Hamriyah Beach as a precaution.
"The reported oil spill off Umm Al Quwain is a serious environmental concern. The temporary closure of beaches and coastal areas is a prudent precaution while the extent of the spill and the movement of the oil are assessed," Nidal Hilal, Professor of Engineering and Director of New York University Abu Dhabi's Water Research Center, told Reuters.
In Ras Al Khaimah, known for its beaches and luxury resorts, authorities said on Saturday that all beaches in the emirate would be closed until further notice.
The UAE's marine life "is rich in fish, plants and corals, with over 500 different species of fish inhabiting the Gulf waters," including dolphins and marine turtles, the International Union for Conservation of Nature, or IUCN, says on its website.
(Reuters - Reporting by Vinaya K and Federico Maccioni, Editing by William Maclean)

item.title: Wildfire scorches more than 500,000 hectares in eastern Mongolia - Qazinform
item.summary: Satellite mapping based on Sentinel-2 imagery, which provides a spatial resolution of 10 meters, showed that the total area affected by the wildfire ...
item.page_text:
A wildfire that broke out on October 8 has affected more than 504,000 hectares of land in and around Mongolia’s Numrug Strictly Protected Area, including 76.4% of the protected territory, according to official data, Qazinform News Agency cites MONTSAME .
The fire affected 448,993.6 hectares of the 587,744.1-hectare protected area located in Khalkhgol soum, Dornod aimag. An additional 55,966.8 hectares outside the protected zone were also affected, the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change of Mongolia confirmed.
Satellite mapping based on Sentinel-2 imagery, which provides a spatial resolution of 10 meters, showed that the total area affected by the wildfire reached 504,960.4 hectares.
The mapping was conducted by the Satellite Applications and Remote Sensing Division of the Institute of Meteorology, Hydrology, and Environmental Research under the National Agency for Meteorology and Environmental Monitoring.
Meanwhile, a specialized working group has been deployed to assess the damage caused by the wildfire in the Numrug Strictly Protected Area. The team includes forensic experts and specialists in forestry and plant research.
The working group has organized the necessary equipment and power supply to support field operations. Experts are conducting assessments at designated locations using two helicopters to evaluate the impact of the fire.
Earlier, Qazinform reported the main blaze had been contained at the Seoul shantytown fire, with no casualties reported.

item.title: Yemen's Houthi Rebels Strike Saudi Aramco's Ras Tanura Oil Terminal
item.summary: Yemen's Houthi Rebels Strike Saudi Aramco's Ras Tanura Oil Terminal. Ras Tanura The oil complex at Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia (Copernicus / Sentinel-2 ).
item.page_text:
By The Maritime Executive 2026-10-27 17:43:08
Yemen's Houthi rebels claim to have hit the Saudi energy complex at Ras Tanura, a gigantic refinery and loading terminal that handles an outsize share of the world's oil supply. It is the latest strike deep into the heart of Saudi territory, and it targeted one of the most valuable locations in the kingdom's energy-centric economy.
"The Houthis have turned Saudi infrastructure into target practice with remarkably little resistance. From airports to critical energy infrastructure, virtually nothing appears beyond their reach," Obsidian Risk Advisors principal Brett Erickson told Al-Monitor. "That is an extraordinarily dangerous position for the global energy market to be in."
Saudi forces claimed to have intercepted three ballistic missiles and four drones launched by Houthi forces on Tuesday, without officially confirming any damage. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree claimed a hit on the Ras Tanura complex, and heat signatures observed by NASA FIRMS satellite sensing on Tuesday indicate a fire at the Ras Tanura export terminal. A source confirmed to Bloomberg that the site had been hit, and said that the fire had been contained. The extent of any damage is as-yet unclear, and the source did not confirm additional claims of a strike on Ras Tanura's refinery.
Get the latest maritime news delivered to your inbox daily.
In addition to the attack on the principal Saudi loading port on the Gulf, the Houthis have attempted to strike Riyadh's international airport multiple times this week, as well as the vulnerable and strategically-vital East-West Pipeline. Previous strikes temporarily disabled the pipeline by damaging pumping stations; Saudi Aramco was able to reactivate it at a reduced flow rate within days, and is said to have a large stockpile of spare parts for its pump systems to swiftly reconstitute export capacity.
France, Britain, Egypt and Pakistan have all pledged varying levels of assistance to help Saudi Arabia fend off Houthi strikes. So far, the Trump administration has declined Saudi requests for aid; the U.S. military is actively engaged in operations in the Strait of Hormuz, and that campaign has reportedly expended the majority of America's missile-interceptor stockpile, leaving less available to provide an air-defense umbrella for U.S. partners.
